The respondent purchased the business of the respondent firm under the name All India Trading Company. The business carried on by the respondent was assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ in the nature of certiorari to quash the orders of the Commercial Tax Officer and the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from his predecessor in title, (ii) the respondent had not been assessed to sales Tax and the Board had no jurisdiction to issue a writ in respect of the same. HELD: The respondent was not a party to the instrument. The respondent was a dealer in the business of a dealer. The respondent had no right to claim the sales tax from the respondent. The respondent did not have any right to claim any sales tax. The respondent could not claim the sales Tax due from his successor in title. [669 B C] The respondent was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to Sales tax in respect thereof. The respondent undertook to pay not only Sch. I liabilities but also other liabilities like sales tax imposed in regard to the business. It was not a case of a dealer who was not a dealer. The respondents, who were the owners of coal mines, were granted a lease of coal and coal mining rights in respect of 400 bighas of land in village Kujama to Satya Karan Banerjee and Girish Chandra Samanta. The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was charged with criminal misappropriation of Rs. 51, and the prosecution was convicted under section 465, Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that there was in fact no person of the name of Parma, that the thumb impression found in the acquittance roll was that of the appellant himself, that he had included a fictitious name in the acquit tance roll, and that the prosecution had not established that the amount drawn by him did not reach the hands of Parma. The prosecution relied on the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and the evidence of P. W. 1, the Sub Divisional Officer, who was the Sub Divisional officer, who was in charge of the work of the appellant. The High Court acquitted the appellant of the charge under section 465 of the Indian Penal Code, but convicted him under section 465 and section 409 of the Indian penal Code. The High court, on appeal, held that the prosecution was not proved that the amount was drawn by the appellant himself and that the conviction was illegal. Held, that the conviction of the appellant was illegal. The conviction was illegal as sanction had not been obtained under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for his prosecution. The conviction of the accused under section 465 was illegal. It was not necessary to consider whether on the evidence, the offence of criminal misappropriation or forgery was committed by the accused or not. The prosecution was not able to establish that the amount in the course of his official duties was misappropriated or misappropriated by the accused. The prosecution had not proved that it was misappropriated or misapplied the accused. In the present case, the prosecution had failed to establish that it was the appellant himself who had misappropriated the amount. The appellant was charged with the offence under section 465. The prosecution did not prove that the amount received by the appellant was in the course or that it was in the hands of the accused. It was for the prosecution to prove that the money was misappropriated or was in the possession of the accused or that it had been misappropriated or misapplication of the money entrusted to him. The appellant had not been able to establish the fact that the money had been misappropriated. The prosecution could not prove that it was so. The appellant could not be convicted under section 466, Indian Penal code. The appellant did not claim to have spent the amount in his course of official duties, but stated that the money did not reach him. The prosecution must prove that the appellant was guilty under section 465 Indian Penal Code and that the appellant had not committed the offence. The appellant admitted that he had not been convicted under section 471, Indian Penal. Code. The appellant, therefore, was not guilty under section 466. The conviction could not be sustained. The appellant must be acquitted. The conviction must be quashed.

The High court, however, held that the appellants had been falsely implicated in the case. The High 'Court, however, relied on the evidence of P.W. 1 and P.Ws. 2 and 3 and held that the prosecution was not able to prove that they were dacoits themselves. The High. Court also held that the evidence of D.W. 2 and D.Ws 2 and 3 was not reliable and that the evidence was not reliable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the presumption that they were innocent must be drawn from the circumstances of the case and that the presumption should be drawn from those circumstances. HELD: The presumption that they are innocent must be accepted. The presumption is stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed. The reasons are obvious. Disposal of the fruits, of crime requires the finding of a person ready to receive them from another person a large quantity of cloth. The appellant, a lessee of a private land, was notified under section 3 of the Madras Estate (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, to be a lessee of the land. The appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Rajah to him. The Collector, on the same day, granted a lease for twenty years to the appellant. On the expiry of the fifth year, the Rajah granted a lease to the appellant for a period of 20 years commencing from February 1, 1947, and ending on November 30, 1947. On December 10, 1947 the appellant applied to be confirmed by the Rajah on the ground that the lease was not a lease within the meaning of the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The appellant contended that the lease could not be terminated by the Government, and that the lease had been terminated by the State Government on December 10,1947, and that it was not a case of a lease within section 20(2) of the Act. Held, that the lease in question was not a 'lease ' within the meaning Of section 20(3) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and conversion into Ryotwar) Act, 1938, and was not a "lease" within the meaning ofs.20(1) Of the Act. The second proviso to the section, which is a self contained proviso, is not a self contained provision and the aid of the third proviso is wholly uncalled for. The second Proviso to the section is not a " lease" within the definition of the term in section 20(4) of the Mines Act, 1952. The second and third proviso deal with the termination of rights created after July 1, 1945, and the second proviso deals with the termination by the Government of the lease. The second part of the proviso deals with a situation where the Government has no power to terminate the lease and the lessee has no right to terminate the rights created after the lease is determined under the second proviso. The second, proviso deals with termination of rights in anticipation of the impending legislation and hence it is not a lease.
